get.description:
A friendly landing response at the base URL.

Useful after deployment: opening the service URL confirms the API is alive
and points you straight at the interactive documentation.

Describe an invite, so the signup page can say "Join Acme as Manager" and
prefill (and lock) the email field.

the invite email already told its recipient.

post.description:
Verify credentials and issue an access + refresh token pair.

Remember the email arrives as `form_data.username` -- an OAuth2 convention,
not a mistake.

Sign out, server side.

Two things are revoked, each if supplied:
    * the ACCESS token in the Authorization header -> denylisted by jti
      until it would have expired anyway
    * the REFRESH token in the body -> its whole sign-in family revoked

Always 204, even when there was nothing valid to revoke. Logout is
idempotent, and a client that is signing out does not need to know its
token had already expired.

Set a new password using the emailed token.

On success EVERY existing session of the account ends: refresh tokens are
revoked and `password_changed_at` makes outstanding access tokens fail.
The usual reason to reset a password is suspecting someone else knows it.

Email a single-use reset link.

THE RESPONSE IS IDENTICAL WHETHER OR NOT THE EMAIL HAS AN ACCOUNT. If it
differed, this endpoint would let anyone test which addresses are
registered. The email itself is sent in the background, after the reply,
so the response time does not give it away either.

Exchange a valid refresh token for a fresh access + refresh pair.

The presented token is REVOKED and a new one issued in the same family
("rotation"). Presenting a token that was already rotated means two
parties hold copies of it -- so the whole family is revoked and both must
sign in again. See models/refresh_token.py.

Register a new user: create an organization, or join one by invite.

Returns `UserOut`, which contains no password field of any kind -- see
schemas/user.py for why that omission is a real security control.

post.description:
Ask a question and get an AI answer grounded in the project's documents.

This is the endpoint the entire project was built to serve. The pipeline
itself is `_answer_events` above; this endpoint runs it to the end and
returns the final result as one JSON reply.

Ask a question and receive the answer as a stream of Server-Sent Events.

Everything that can be REFUSED is checked here, before the stream starts
-- ownership (404), the rate limit and the token quota (429) -- so a
refusal is an ordinary HTTP error the client handles like any other.
Once streaming has begun the status is already 200, so a later failure
arrives as an `error` event instead.

WHY THE STREAM OPENS ITS OWN DATABASE SESSION
The request's session (deps.get_db) belongs to the request handler, and
may be closed as soon as this function RETURNS -- which is before the
stream has produced its first byte. The generator therefore opens a
session of its own, and closes it when the stream ends.

get.description:
Download or view the ORIGINAL uploaded file.

Useful for verifying a citation: read the AI's answer, then open the source
document and confirm it for yourself.

Note the access check goes through the document's PROJECT. A document has
no `org_id` of its own -- ownership is always established by walking up the
chain, exactly as the vector search does.

post.description:
Process a document again from its stored file (editor+, audited).

WHEN YOU WANT THIS
  * it failed, and the cause has since been fixed (OCR installed, a
    provider key added);
  * EMBEDDING_PROVIDER or the model changed -- retrieval only compares
    vectors from the CURRENT model, so older documents stop matching
    until they are re-embedded;
  * you want different chunking (pass chunk_strategy / chunk_size /
    chunk_overlap in the body).

The document goes back to "pending" and leaves search until it is
"completed" again; the pipeline (tasks/ingestion.py, stage 4) deletes
the old chunks before writing the new ones, so nothing is duplicated.
Returns 202 for the same reason the upload does.

RE-INDEX RESUMES. On a FAILED or PAUSED document whose chunks were all
saved with the same chunk settings, the pipeline does not start again:
it skips straight to embedding the chunks that have no vector yet. So
"failed at 900 of 1,200" continues from 901. A completed document, or
new chunk settings, rebuild from the file. A paused document (waiting
for the embedding rate limit) may be re-indexed to resume it NOW.

get.description:
Confirm the API is running, and report how the AI layer is configured.

Hosting platforms poll an endpoint like this to decide whether the service
is healthy. Reporting the AI configuration here is a deliberate debugging
aid: after deploying, one request tells you whether the server actually
picked up your GROQ_API_KEY, which is by far the most common thing to get
wrong in a cloud environment.

READINESS: can this instance serve real traffic right now?

Checks the database, Redis and (with INGESTION_MODE=celery) that a Celery
worker answers a ping -- concurrently, each with its own timeout -- and
reports each component's status. Answers 503 when a HARD dependency is
down, so a load balancer or deploy can hold traffic back.

/health above deliberately checks nothing: see core/health.py for why
liveness and readiness must be separate.

delete.description:
Delete a project and EVERYTHING in it.

WHAT GOES, AND WHO REMOVES IT
    documents, chunks, embeddings,   the database, through ON DELETE
    chat sessions and messages       CASCADE on every foreign key -- one
                                     DELETE of the project row
    the stored files                 this endpoint, AFTER the commit

WHY THE FILES GO AFTER THE COMMIT
If the transaction failed after the files were already deleted, the
database would still list documents whose bytes are gone. Deleting them
after the commit can at worst leave an orphaned file -- invisible to
every user, and harmless -- never a visible document with no content.

`AsyncResult` reads the job's status from the Celery result backend --

is why a task whose result has expired (we set a 1-day TTL) reports as
PENDING again.

Queue a job that adds two numbers after a short pause.

The simplest possible end-to-end proof that the queue works: API -> Redis
-> worker -> result -> API. Use it first whenever background processing
appears to be stuck.

Queue a SIMULATED document pipeline.

This runs the fake task in tasks/test.py, which just prints each stage and
sleeps. It touches no files and no database, so it verifies that a
multi-step job runs to completion without needing a real upload.

The REAL pipeline is `process_document_task` in tasks/ingestion.py, and it
is triggered automatically by the upload endpoint -- not from here.

get.description:
Return the currently authenticated user's profile.

There is no database query in the body, because the dependency has already
done all the work: it decoded and verified the token, loaded the user, and
confirmed the account is active. All that remains is to return the object.

`response_model=UserOut` is doing something important here. `current_user`
is a full `User` row and DOES carry `hashed_password`, but `UserOut` does
not declare that field, so Pydantic drops it. The hash cannot leak, because
exposing it would require deliberately adding it to the schema.
